statement: Kimpa Vita (baptized Dona Beatriz), a young Kongolese noblewoman, claimed in 1704 to have died and been reincarnated/possessed by Saint Anthony of Padua, preaching that Jesus, Mary, and the saints were themselves Kongolese/African, and criticizing Italian Capuchin missionaries for excluding Black sainthood. Her movement arose amid civil wars over the Kongo throne following the 1665 Battle of Mbwila; John K. Thornton (The Kongolese Saint Anthony, Cambridge UP, 1998) reads it as substantially a peace movement functioning as "something of a theocracy," aimed at ending the wars and restoring unified sacralized kingship — a REFORM of Kongo Christianity from within, not an import of a new tradition. She was executed by burning in 1706 on orders connected to King Pedro IV, with Capuchin missionary involvement in her heresy condemnation.

sources.citation: Thornton, John K. The Kongolese Saint Anthony: Dona Beatriz Kimpa Vita and the Antonian Movement, 1684-1706. Cambridge University Press, 1998.
sources.author: John K. Thornton

notes: No surviving African-authored primary source exists; the documentary record consists entirely of accounts by hostile Capuchin missionary witnesses (Bernardo da Gallo, Lorenzo da Lucca) — Thornton's methodological contribution is reading these "against the grain."
